Das germanische Betonungsgesetz, nach dem der Hauptakzent auf die erste Stammsilbe fällt, macht sich in zusammengesetzten Wörtern darin bemerkbar, daß das zweite, nebentonige Kompositionsglied vielfach geschwächt wird, so in: öbrmarxdl Obermarchtal, duidl (Opp.) Tiefental, hoedne Heidenheim, ladss Lonsee, khirbe Kirchweih, noxbr Nachbar (zu der Vollform noxbaur s. new_statements.translation: § 58. Shortening in compounds. The Germanic stress law, according to which the main accent falls on the first stem syllable, makes itself felt in compound words in that the second, secondarily stressed member of the compound is frequently weakened, e.g. öbrmarxdl 'Obermarchtal', duidl 'Tiefental', hoedne 'Heidenheim', ladss 'Lonsee', khirbe 'Kirchweih', noxbr 'Nachbar' (beside the full form noxbaur), hédse 'Handschuhe', wisfl 'wieviel', fodl 'Vorteil', fäsnad 'Fastnacht', medek 'Montag', däesdek 'Dienstag', mid 'Mittwoch', dösdek 'Donnerstag', foidek 'Feiertag' (cf. Bopp p. 79; Kauffmann §§ 101, 102).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main word stress falls on the first syllable of the stem (root-initial, Germanic pattern); in compounds the first member carries main stress and the second, secondarily stressed member is reduced (Montag > medek). Inflectional/derivational prefixes ge-, be-, ver- are unstressed and in this dialect mostly non-syllabic (gmaxd 'gemacht', blegd 'belegt', frirnad 'verirrt', same page), so native words are in effect initial-stressed. Corroboration: Bopp 1890:45-46 (Münsingen) treats first-syllable stress as the norm from which only given names deviate; Hiller 2003 (snippet only) states Swabian has no contrastive stress, native stems have a single stressable vowel, and loanwords are adapted with weight-insensitive initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Second members of compounds are 'nebentonig' (secondary-stressed) and frequently phonetically weakened/shortened (Strohmaier §58); Kauffmann 1890 §39 Anm.2 adds that Swabian compound members differ only minimally in expiratory strength, without the NHG main/secondary cut distinction. Frey 1975 (snippet) distinguishes Hauptton, Nebenton, unbetont.
new_statements.exceptions: Given names (Bopp 1890 §19: mrai 'Marie', annamrai, and hypocoristics from non-initial parts: rika < Friedrike, sdofl < Christoph) may not have initial stress; griasgot/phiagot 'Grüss Gott/Behüt Gott' vary between initial and second-syllable stress with a pragmatic nuance (Bopp p.21); loanwords: Hiller 2003 reports initial stress replacing source-language non-initial stress, Wagner 1889 lists loans with pretonic syllables (abodek 'Apotheke', grogodil 'Krokodil').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement framed via the Germanic stress law as operative in the Blaubeuren (Oberamt Blaubeuren, Alb/Danube) local Swabian dialect; evidence drawn from compound reduction in citation forms and place names. Not a dedicated stress chapter; modern dedicated treatments (Frey 1975 §Betonung, Russ 1990, Caro Reina 2019 ch.7, Hiller 2003) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes the local Swabian dialect of the Oberamt Blaubeuren (Swabian Alb / upper Danube, East-/Middle-Swabian), which falls under swab1242 (Glottolog has no separate code for it). Supporting older sources describe Münsingen (Bopp 1890) and Reutlingen (Wagner 1889) Swabian; Kügler 2005 and Frey 1975 describe Stuttgart urban Swabian; Hiller 2003 describes Swabian generally (author's native variety). All are swab1242.

sources.note: Intonation of Stuttgart Swabian (default L*H L%, low accented syllable with following rise). §2.2.1 pp.15-16 lists segmental dialect features only; ch.4 pp.65-67 reviews Frey 1975:67f. No statement of where lexical stress falls; Standard-German-type word stress is presupposed in the accent analysis.

sources.note: pp.45-46 §19 'Betonung der Namen': only given names deviate from the usual stressing; 'Die betonung der ersten silbe, wie sie für das oberdeutsche angenommen wird, ist nicht durchgängig' (khatre 'Katharine', rege 'Regine', gregoore 'Gregorius' initial-stressed, but mrai 'Marie' etc. point to non-initial stress); p.21 griasgot/phiagot may be stressed on either syllable with a pragmatic difference.

sources.citation: Kauffmann, Friedrich. 1890. Geschichte der schwäbischen Mundart im Mittelalter und in der Neuzeit. Strassburg: Trübner (archive.org geschichtedersch00kaufuoft, scanned text).
sources.note: §§38-40 'Accentuirung' (pp.20-22) treat the nature of the accent only: ictus syllables carry weakly-cut accent and low tone rising c. two tones to the following weak syllable; §39 Anm.2: in nominal compounds Swabian lacks the NHG main/secondary (strong-cut/weak-cut) distinction, both members differ only minimally in expiratory strength. Placement (stem syllable) is presupposed, not stated.
